title: Zeno's lost books
hookLine: Zeno wrote many books, almost all lost; we know him through others (Diogenes Laërtius 7)

cards: An ancient biographer copied out a long list of one man's book titles. Not one of those books can be found today.
All anyone knows of their author comes from what others said about him, centuries later, some who never met him, some of them rivals. That's the man who started it all.

For months this path has read Epictetus, Seneca and Marcus, the Roman Stoics, whose words survived. Now it widens to the school before them, and begins with its founder, whose words almost all vanished.

teach.h: FROM CITIUM, BY WAY OF A SHIPWRECK.
teach.b: First, who he was. Zeno came from Citium, a town on Cyprus, and made his way to Athens.
The story, told by the biographer Diogenes Laërtius, is that he was a merchant who lost his cargo in a shipwreck, and in Athens found philosophy.

He studied with the Cynic Crates and others, then taught in a painted colonnade on the edge of the marketplace, the Stoa Poikilē. His followers were called the people of the stoa, the porch: Stoics. Second, the books.

teach.h: A LIST OF TITLES, NONE SURVIVING.
teach.b: Diogenes lists Zeno's titles in book seven of his Lives: a Republic, On Life according to Nature, On the Passions, On What Is Appropriate, On Law, and more. Not one survives whole.
What's left are scraps: a sentence quoted here, a summary there, mostly by later writers, some of them critics.
Third, what that means. Everything this path has called Stoicism this year comes from people writing centuries after Zeno.
The founder is known the way you know a great-great-grandparent: through stories, a few sayings, and family resemblance.
And some of his ideas, especially parts of his Republic, were apparently embarrassing to later Stoics, who may have smoothed them over. Fourth, the strange comfort.
Zeno's words mostly vanished, and the school was still alive centuries later, when Marcus wrote. What survived wasn't his sentences. It was what his students did with them.

how: Students of Stoicism read Zeno through the fragments and reports gathered from later writers, especially Diogenes Laërtius's Lives, book seven.

practice: Suppose that a hundred years from now almost nothing you made survives: no files, no photos, only what people remember of how you were.

Ask what you'd want carried on, not a sentence or an achievement but a way of being: patient with your kids, honest at work, the friend who showed up. Let one thing come forward, and hold it for a few breaths.

wordCard.voice: Zeno, the shipwrecked merchant who found philosophy in Athens and taught in a painted colonnade, though almost none of his own books survive. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: the painted porch in Athens where Zeno taught, which gave the Stoics their name.
